top_cited_works.title: The effect of the formulation of nonlinear terms on aliasing errors in spectral methods
Compressibility effects on the growth and structure of homogeneous turbulent shear flow
top_cited_works.abstract: Compressibility effects within decaying isotropic turbulence and homogeneous turbulent shear flow have been studied using direct numerical simulation. The objective of this work is to increase our understanding of compressible turbulence and to aid the development of turbulence models for compressible flows. The numerical simulations of compressible isotropic turbulence show that compressibility effects are highly dependent on the initial conditions. The shear flow simulations, on the other hand, show that measures of compressibility evolve to become independent of their initial values and are parameterized by the root mean square Mach number. The growth rate of the turbulence in compressible homogeneous shear flow is reduced compared to that in the incompressible case. The reduced growth rate is the result of an increase in the dissipation rate and energy transfer to internal energy by the pressure–dilatation correlation. Examination of the structure of compressible homogeneous shear flow reveals the presence of eddy shocklets, which are important for the increased dissipation rate of compressible turbulence.

top_cited_works.title: Overview of Turbulent Inflow Boundary Conditions for Large-Eddy Simulations
top_cited_works.abstract: Generating realistic turbulent inflow conditions for large-eddy simulations and other large-scale-resolving approaches is essential to fully exploit the ever-increasing capabilities of modern computers in solving fluid flow problems of engineering interest. This research area has received much attention during the last two decades and will continue to grow as large-eddy simulation is applied to an even wider range of flows. It is deceptively difficult to generate turbulent inflow fluctuations that are realistic for a specific problem, and various methods have been designed to improve this realism. A review of such turbulent inflow boundary conditions is presented, broadly classified into transition-inducing approaches, turbulence library-based methods, recycling–rescaling-based methods, and synthetic turbulence generators. The last category is given more attention to cover a variety of creative approaches that are found in the literature as well as due to its practicality for problems of industrial interest. recent_works.title: Performance Analysis of an Unsteady Ejector Driven by Exhaust Conditions of a Rotating Detonation Engine (RDE)
recent_works.abstract: The goal of this project is to assess the performance and mixing characteristics of unsteady ejectors driven by a rotating detonation engine (RDE), using 3D unsteady RANS simulations and detached eddy simulations (DES). These simulations will incorporate the azimuthal variations in flow properties and the azimuthal component of velocity at the exit plane of an RDE, characteristics often neglected in similar computational studies. As a precursor to these studies, preliminary axisymmetric RANS calculations have been performed, neglecting azimuthal variation in flow properties and the azimuthal component of velocity. The motivation behind these preliminary calculations is to show proof of concept and serve as a foundation for the subsequent high-fidelity three-dimensional simulations. The flow conditions at the exit of the RDE are obtained using a Method of Characteristics (MOC) solver, which provides realistic two-dimensional steady-state solution of the unwrapped RDE. Results from these calculations indicate that the ejector is capable of significantly attenuating the oscillations of the RDE exhaust. recent_works.title: Large-Eddy Simulation of an Axisymmetric Shock-Wave/Boundary-Layer Interaction at Mach 2.5
recent_works.abstract: Implicit large-eddy simulation (ILES) of a turbulent, axisymmetric, shock-wave/boundary- layer interaction was performed at Mach 2.5. The simulation was performed to compare to recent experimental work completed at NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) under the Turbulent Computational Fluid Dynamics Validation Experiment (TCFDVE). The circular test section of the TCFDVE allows shock-wave/boundary-layer interactions to be studied without corner effects. The ILES was completed using a low-dissipation, hybrid advection scheme available in VULCAN-CFD which blends a fourth-order symmetric reconstruction with a third-order upwind-biased MUSCL scheme. The method of recycling/rescaling was used to generate a scale-resolved turbulent boundary layer. To save on computational cost, a Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) solution was imposed at some boundary conditions. Comparison to experimental data showed promising results. PIV, Pitot, wall static pressure taps, and hot-wire data were used for comparison. recent_works.title: Machine Learning for Practical Real-Time Test Campaign Design
recent_works.abstract: Efficient test campaign design is essential for rapidly validating and verifying aerospace systems. This paper proposes an approach utilizing Support Vector Machines (SVMs) to optimize the design of hypersonic test campaigns in real time. SVMs are employed to predict the utility of candidate test configurations based on datasets acquired a priori. The proposed methodology aims to enhance the efficiency of test campaign design by identifying configurations most likely to yield informative data, which has the potential to reduce resource expenditure and accelerate the pace at which a researcher can acquire valuable experimental and computational data. This paper presents the formulation of SVM-based predictive models tailored to the unique requirements of the Boeing/AFOSR Mach-6 Quiet Tunnel (BAM6QT), detailing the feature selection process and model training. Heat transfer over a finite-span compression ramp on a sliced 7 degree half-angle cone is used as a configuration of investigation for SVM training. recent_works.title: Background-oriented-schlieren-based optical velocimetry of low-convective-Mach-number turbulent shear layers
recent_works.abstract: Abstract Background-oriented schlieren (BOS)-based velocimetry is a potential method for achieving simultaneous measurements of density and velocity in a flow with density gradients. Similar to schlieren velocimetry, BOS velocimetry relies on (1) refraction of light due to density gradients and (2) the presence of turbulent eddies or contrast by high-/low-density fluid parcels to serve as seeding particles. Previous attempts at BOS velocimetry suffered from compounded noise, error propagation, and significant loss of spatial resolution due to the requirement for an additional round of interrogation. Kymography-based BOS velocimetry has been shown to produce accurate velocity measurements but at the expense of spatiotemporally averaging the flow field. The optical flow displacement estimation method was shown to be ineffective to yield useful velocity information for schlieren velocimetry, due to the large displacements of turbulent eddies between adjacent time instances.
